text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish Newtonian estimates from results supplied by general relativity. 01Special relativity: a light clock and Pythagoras Imagine a clock made of light bouncing between mirrors. In its rest frame, a one-way trip covers ℓ in t₀ = ℓ/c. An observer seeing the clock move sideways at speed v sees a diagonal light path. Both measure light speed c. A moving light clock makes a triangleCompare one-way trips between mirrors. The right panel shows the lower mirror at departure and upper mirror at arrival, with horizontal travel vt and mirror spacing ℓ. At the same light speed c, the longer diagonal path takes a longer inertial-frame time t.View larger diagram ↗ (ct)2 = ℓ2 + (vt)2 ⇒ t = t0√(1−v2/c2) For these same two clock events, the inertial-frame interval t exceeds the moving clock’s proper interval t₀. This is special-relativistic time dilation, distinct from gravitational time dilation. 02Estimate escape speed using Newtonian mechanics 12mvesc2 = GMmR ⇒ vesc = √(2GMR) Formally setting vesc = c yields R = 2GM/c². But mv²/2 is not the kinetic energy of a photon. This is a clue to a length scale, not a derivation of a relativistic horizon. 03The relativistic result: Schwarzschild radius rs = 2GMc2 ≈ 2.95 (MM☉) km General relativity describes gravity through spacetime geometry. Its solution for a nonrotating, uncharged, spherical black hole identifies this radius as an event horizon. Future-directed light and matter inside cannot reach the distant exterior. Deriving that spacetime solution is outside our scope. Matching the same radius by substituting c into escape speed does not derive black holes from Newtonian mechanics. The match alone does not establish spacetime’s causal structure. 04Compare stationary clocks in a gravitational field ΔτΔt = √(1−rsr) (r > rs) Δτ is the time recorded by a stationary clock at r; Δt corresponds to a stationary clock far away. This equation is supplied by the relativistic solution. At r = 2rs, the ratio is √(1/2) ≈ 0.707. During an interval corresponding to one hour far away, the stationary local clock advances about 42.4 minutes. A stationary clock cannot be placed at r = rs, and this stationary-clock expression does not apply inside. An infalling observer can cross the horizon in finite proper time. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Would a black hole of one solar mass pull a distant planet more strongly than the Sun? Show the answer and reasoning At the same distant radius in spherical symmetry, the gravity depends on the same mass. What differs is the compactness and the presence of an event horizon.
